title: Infra GPU Fleet: CI/CD, IaC, Cloud Accounts & Networking Runbook (2026)
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates operational standards and runbooks for Redwood's GPU fleet and related infrastructure: Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines for infra, cloud accounts and networking patterns, and capacity runbooks. Target audience: infra engineers, SRE, platform, and on-call. This doc is an operational reference (not a design deep dive) and includes ownership, SLOs, alert thresholds, example Terraform usage, CI/CD recipes, and step-by-step incident/runbook procedures.

Scope
- GPU node pools (hosted and dedicated clusters)
- Terraform modules that manage cloud accounts, VPCs, subnets, and GPU nodegroups
- CI/CD pipelines that lint, plan, and apply infra changes
- Networking patterns for private deployments and VPC peering
- Runbooks for capacity shortages, node failures, and kernel/driver issues

Ownership and Contacts
- Infra Ownership: GPU Fleet Team (oncall rotation). Primary: asha.patel@redwood.com
- IaC Modules: Modules Team (owner: daniel.kim@redwood.com)
- CI/CD Pipelines: Platform CI Team (owner: meera.singh@redwood.com)
- Networking & Cloud Accounts: Cloud Network Team (owner: liam.oconnor@redwood.com)

High-level Architecture
- Per-region VPC per-account, segmented by environment (prod/dedicated/staging).
- GPU nodepools are managed as autoscaling node groups (cloud-provider autoscale + cluster-autoscaler) with mixed instance types and spot instance fallback pools.
- Terraform control plane (terraform-cloud / org workspace) for state management and policy enforcement (Sentinel/OPA).
- CI/CD: PR -> plan -> gated approval (for prod) -> apply. All applies logged with run metadata.

IaC Modules (reference)
| Module | Repo | Owner | Description |
|--------|------|-------|-------------|
| modules/gpu-nodegroup | git://infra-modules/gpu-nodegroup | daniel.kim | Creates managed nodegroups with instance selection, GPU drivers, and node labeling. |
| modules/vpc-core | git://infra-modules/vpc-core | liam.oconnor | VPC, subnets, route tables, NATs, peering and egress firewall rules. |
| modules/cloud-accounts | git://infra-modules/cloud-accounts | cloud-network-team | Account bootstrap (roles, SCPs, permission boundaries) and cross-account roles. |
| modules/iam-roles | git://infra-modules/iam-roles | security | Centralized IAM roles for infra services. |

Recommended Terraform usage (example)
```hcl
module "gpu_nodegroup" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@infra-modules/gpu-nodegroup.git//modules/gpu-nodegroup"
  cluster_id = module.eks.cluster_id
  instance_types = ["g5.2xlarge", "g5.4xlarge"]
  gpu_driver_version = "535.86"
  desired_capacity = 10
  max_capacity = 80
}

# plan and apply pipeline runs terraform fmt -> validate -> plan -> apply (with kept state on terraform-cloud)
```

CI/CD Patterns and Pipeline Steps
- Branch naming: feature/infra/<short-desc> or hotfix/infra/<ticket>
- Pre-merge checks: terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec, unit tests for modules, policy checks.
- Plan: PR comment contains full plan output and diff summary.
- Apply gating: non-prod auto-apply; prod requires 2 approvals (infra lead + security) and a scheduled maintenance window unless flagged as emergency.
- Pipeline tooling: GitHub Actions or Buildkite runners in a dedicated infra CI account.

Cloud Accounts & Networking Standards
- Per-environment accounts: prod, staging, dedicated-customer, dev. Root-level guardrails via SCPs.
- VPC design: 3 AZs, public/private subnets, NAT gateway per-AZ (or central NAT depending on cost/perf), default NACLs restrictive.
- Peering and transit: use Transit Gateway for multi-account connectivity; avoid manual peering at scale.
- Private deployments: customer VPCs use VPC peering or TGW attachments with strict route filters and allowlist for control-plane endpoints.
- Egress: all GPU workloads must route egress through our allowed egress proxies for audit and caching.

GPU Fleet & Capacity Management
- Supported instance families: G5/G4/GPUs on provider X (also supports L4 on provider Y for low-cost inference).
- Sizing guidance: aim for per-node GPU utilization 40-70% for stable throughput; short peaks up to 85% acceptable.
- Autoscaling policies:
  - Cloud autoscale: target 50% node GPU utilization across nodegroup; min 2 nodes per AZ for prod.
  - Cluster-autoscaler / scheduler: scale up when pending pods request GPUs and nodegroup capacity cannot satisfy.
- Capacity planning cadence:
  - Monthly capacity review (capacity and quota requests) owner: GPU Fleet PM.
  - Quarterly reserved capacity forecast for Dedicated customers.

SLOs, Metrics and Alerting
- Key metrics (per-region / per-nodegroup): GPU_utilization_pct, GPU_memory_used_mb, Node_gpu_temperature_c, Pending_gpu_pods_count, Job_queue_latency_ms.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - P1: Pending_gpu_pods_count > 50 for 5m -> alert paging SRE + GPU team
  - P1: Average GPU_utilization > 90% across prod nodegroups for 10m -> paging
  - P2: Node_gpu_temperature_c > 90C -> page infra oncall, cordon node
  - P2: Failed driver installs > 5 within 1h -> page infra + rollback driver rollout
- Dashboards: per-region GPU fleet dashboard (tail latency, utilization, queue length).

Runbooks (step-by-step)
1) Capacity shortage (Pending pods growing)
  a) Check dashboard and alerts: identify region and nodegroup.
  b) Run: kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep Pending (filter by GPU resources).
  c) If autoscaler not triggering: check cluster-autoscaler logs and cloud provider quotas.
  d) Temporary mitigation: manually increase nodegroup desired_capacity by +20% (apply via terraform var override in staging workspace or cloud console for emergency).
  e) Longer-term: open quota request with cloud provider (owner: cloud-network-team).

2) Node GPU driver failures after rollout
  a) Detect via alert (Failed driver installs).
  b) Immediately stop rollout in pipeline, rollback to previous driver version via terraform module param and trigger a rolling update.
  c) Cordon affected nodes and drain: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
  d) If widespread, trigger emergency rollback and restore snapshot for critical workloads.

3) Node OOM / kernel panic
  a) Identify node via node exporter / metrics.
  b) If node unrecoverable, cordon and cordonforce then recreate via nodegroup replacement.
  c) Postmortem: collect dmesg, journalctl, nvidia-driver logs and file an incident with severity and owner.

Change Management and Rollouts
- Canary policy: small canary (% of nodes or single AZ) for kernel/driver/agent changes; minimum 5 nodes in canary for GPU drivers.
- Rollout steps:
  1) Publish change in RFC with impact analysis and rollback plan.
  2) Create pipeline PR with module changes and smoke tests.
  3) Run canary (apply to staging then one AZ in prod). Monitor for 30m to 2h depending on change class.
  4) If no regressions, proceed to full rollout in waves (AZ-by-AZ).

Operational Playbook (Quick Commands)
- Terraform plan (CI): terraform workspace select prod && terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
- Force scale nodegroup (emergency): aws eks update-nodegroup-config --cluster-name CLUSTER --nodegroup-name NG --scaling-config minSize=2,maxSize=120,desiredSize=60
- Cordon + drain: kubectl cordon NODE && kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

Runbook Review and Exercises
- Quarterly game-day for capacity failover and spot-fallback scenarios; responsible: GPU Fleet Team.
- Runbook owners must review and sign off annually or after any major incident.
